title_en: Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company v. Zhaoqing Customs — administrative dispute over customs valuation
ruling_gist_en: Where the buyer of imported goods has a special relationship with the overseas seller, such as a branch-head office relationship, joint operation, profit sharing, etc., and the declared price of the imported goods is significantly lower than the comparable actual transaction price of the same model product, or even lower than the production cost, and the declarant cannot prove that the special relationship between the buyer and seller did not affect the transaction price, then, in accordance with Article 55 of the Customs Law and Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures, the Customs may reject the declared price and appraise the dutiable value in accordance with Articles 7 to 11 of the Customs Valuation Measures.
keywords_en: Administrative Law; Customs Valuation Administrative Dispute; First Instance; Intermediate People's Court; Guangdong Province; Legal Person; State Organ; Customs Law; Measures of the Customs for the Examination and Determination of the Duty-paying Value of Import and Export Goods; Whether Special Relationship Affects Transaction Value; Application of Customs Valuation Methods; Authenticity of Declared Price; Low Declared Price of Imported Goods; Special Relationship Between Buyer and Seller; Customs Price Inquiry and Valuation; Administrative Litigation; Zhaoqing Customs Customs Valuation Administrative Dispute
full_text_en:
Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Development Company v. Zhaoqing Customs — Administrative Dispute over Customs Valuation

[Ruling Summary]

Where a special relationship exists between the buyer of imported goods and the overseas seller, such as a branch-head office relationship, joint operation, or profit-sharing arrangement, and the declared price of the imported goods is significantly lower than the actual comparable transaction prices of products of the same model, or even lower than the production cost, if the declarant fails to prove that the special relationship between the buyer and the seller did not affect the transaction price, then, pursuant to Article 55 of the Customs Law and Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures, the Customs may refuse to accept the declared price and shall determine the dutiable value in accordance with Articles 7 to 11 of the Customs Valuation Measures.

Plaintiff: Guangdong Province Zhaoqing City Foreign Trade Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company), domiciled at: Jiangbin West Road, Zhaoqing City.
Legal Representative: Xu Weibiao, General Manager of the Company.
Defendant: Zhaoqing Customs of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as Zhaoqing Customs), domiciled at: Duanzhou Qi Road, Zhaoqing City.
Legal Representative: Huang Jianling, Customs Commissioner of the said Customs.
Third Party: Guangdong Province Zhaoqing City Aosi Science and Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Aosi Technology Company), domiciled at: Gongnong New Village, Zhaoqing City.
Legal Representative: Feng Weiheng, Manager of the Company.

The Plaintiff, Guangdong Province Zhaoqing City Foreign Trade Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company), dissatisfied with the three "Special Value-Added Tax Payment Certificates Collected by Customs" (hereinafter referred to as the three "Tax Payment Certificates") numbered 517720021772499587/L04, 517720021772499588/L03, and 517720021772499589/L03 issued by the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as Zhaoqing Customs) on May 20, 2003, and the four "Customs Valuation Notices" (hereinafter referred to as the four "Valuation Notices") numbered 517720021772499587-1, 517720021772499587-2, 517720021772499588-1, and 517720021772499589-1 issued on May 28, 2003, instituted administrative proceedings with the Zhaoqing Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province. As Zhaoqing City Aosi Science and Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Aosi Technology Company) has a legal interest in the specific administrative act under litigation, the Zhaoqing Intermediate People's Court lawfully added it as a Third Party to participate in the proceedings.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, alleges that the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, issued the three "Tax Payment Certificates" to the Plaintiff without explaining how the price basis for the tax was formed, thereby depriving the Plaintiff of its right to know. Only upon the Plaintiff's application did the Defendant prepare the four "Valuation Notices," stating that because the declared price of the goods was lower than the "price risk parameters" and because there existed a special relationship between the actual domestic buyer and the overseas seller, it suspected the Plaintiff's declared price was untrue and unreasonable, and thus estimated the price in accordance with the provisions of the "Measures of the Customs of the People's Republic of China for Examining and Determining the Dutiable Value of Import and Export Goods" (hereinafter referred to as the Customs Valuation Measures). The "price risk parameters" are merely the average prices of similar products. A declared price lower than this parameter does not demonstrate that it is untrue or unreasonable. Even if a special relationship exists between the buyer and the seller, if the special relationship did not affect the transaction price, on what basis does the Customs suspect the Plaintiff's declared price? To demonstrate that the declared price is true and reasonable, the Plaintiff has already provided the Defendant with a large amount of price data. The Defendant cannot point out any specific issues with this data, yet refuses to accept it and persists in conducting its own valuation. Moreover, it failed to follow the order of priority for applying several methods of determining dutiable value as stipulated in Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures, instead directly applying the so-called "reasonable method." This is erroneous, and the estimated price is arbitrary and fictitious. The three "Tax Payment Certificates" made based on the erroneous valuation are naturally also erroneous. The Plaintiff requests the court to: 1. Revoke the three "Tax Payment Certificates" and the four "Valuation Notices" issued by the Defendant; 2. Order the Defendant to re-determine the price and issue new "Tax Payment Certificates" according to law, and to return the excess tax collected; 3. Order the Defendant to bear all litigation costs of this case.

The Plaintiff submitted as evidence contracts, purchase orders, import goods customs declarations, special value-added tax invoices, special customs payment certificates, etc., entered into between the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, and several other domestic companies.

Defendant's Defense: The Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, argues that, as the state's import and export regulatory authority, the Customs possesses a large amount of price data for similar imported goods based on actual international trade. By collecting data from authoritative websites on commodity prices, the Defendant found that the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company's, declared price was significantly lower than the price risk parameters set by the Customs. Consequently, on November 27, 2002, and April 28, 2003, the Defendant twice issued "Price Inquiry Notices" to the Plaintiff, requesting a written explanation and the provision of relevant materials. Although the Plaintiff and the domestic actual buyer, the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, provided explanations and relevant materials, upon review, the Defendant discovered multiple contradictions and defects in these materials, primarily manifested in: 1. Some value-added tax invoices showed a price inversion where the purchase price was higher than the sale price, which defies common sense. 2. Some purchase orders indicated a price inclusive of tax identical to the price exclusive of tax on the value-added tax invoices, which is illogical. 3. Some materials were provided by companies that had previously been subject to Customs investigations for smuggling, price fraud, or other acts, raising questions about their corporate integrity, and which had transactional relationships with the Third Party; thus, they were insufficient as evidence. During the price inquiry process, the Plaintiff and the Third Party repeatedly acknowledged that a special relationship existed between the Third Party and Hong Kong Aosi Company. However, they failed to explain whether this special relationship affected the transaction price between the parties. Furthermore, the Plaintiff and the Third Party consistently failed to provide materials such as foreign exchange payment records that could directly reflect international trade prices, or international trade price data for the integrated circuit industry. Based on this, the Defendant concluded that the materials provided by the Plaintiff and the Third Party were insufficient to prove that the declared price was true and accurate. Therefore, in accordance with Articles 7 and 11 of the Customs Valuation Measures, since other price methods were inapplicable, the Defendant estimated the dutiable value using a reasonable method based on the Customs' price data and issued the three "Tax Payment Certificates." Given that the price data used as evidence was confidential Customs information and could not be directly provided to the Plaintiff and the Third Party, the Defendant issued the four "Valuation Notices" upon the Plaintiff's request. Although the "Valuation Notices" were issued after the "Tax Payment Certificates," the Defendant had previously informed the Plaintiff of the entire valuation process through the inquiry and consultation procedures, thereby fulfilling its notification obligation according to law. The Plaintiff's claim that the Defendant's estimated price was arbitrary and fictitious and that it was deprived of its right to know is inconsistent with the facts. The three "Tax Payment Certificates" and four "Valuation Notices" issued by the Defendant have clear facts, conclusive evidence, correct application of law, and lawful procedures; the court should uphold this specific administrative act.

The Defendant submitted as evidence the purchase orders, price inquiry sheets, contracts, customs declarations, accompanying invoices, packing lists, confirmations of sale, technical descriptions, value-added tax invoices, investigation records, Price Inquiry Notices, price consultation record sheets, price information collection forms, explanations of the price of imported goods, and confidential internal Customs correspondence, etc., upon which the specific administrative act under litigation was based, as well as the legal bases for its actions, including the "Customs Law of the People's Republic of China" (hereinafter referred to as the Customs Law) and the Customs Valuation Measures.

Third Party's Statement: The Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, states that from November 25, 2002, to June 2003, it provided the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, with detailed price data spanning 153 pages to demonstrate that the price of the imported goods declared by the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, on its behalf was true. However, the Defendant did not actively investigate the authenticity of these materials and rejected them all on the sole ground that "the credibility is low and insufficient to prove the truthfulness and accuracy of the declared price," thereby disregarding the rights of the administrative counterpart. A capital verification report proves that Hong Kong Aosi Company is not a shareholder of the Third Party; the Defendant's finding that a special relationship exists between the Third Party and Hong Kong Aosi Company affecting the transaction price is inconsistent with the objective facts. The Defendant's valuation deviated from the principles established in the Customs Valuation Measures, violated the valuation procedures prescribed therein, and the determined dutiable value lacks factual basis, being an arbitrary and fictitious price. By refusing to submit the basis of its valuation on the grounds of state secrets and commercial secrets, the Defendant deprived the Third Party of its right to know. The Third Party requests the court to order the revocation of the Defendant's valuation administrative act.

The Third Party submitted as evidence the capital verification report issued by Zhaoqing Tianyuan Xinzhan Certified Public Accountants Co., Ltd., a comparison table of Aosi Technology Company's sales, etc.

After cross-examination and authentication, the Zhaoqing Intermediate People's Court finds the following facts:

On November 27, 2002, the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, declared three lots of imported goods to the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, under general trade procedures, including 100,000 units of RC4558DR type integrated circuits manufactured in Mexico, 95,000 units of RC4558P type integrated circuits, 27,500 units of SN74HCU04DR type integrated circuits manufactured in Thailand, and 12,500 units of SN74HCU04DR type integrated circuits manufactured in Malaysia. The declared unit price for all goods was USD 0.05 each.

Upon reviewing the customs declarations and accompanying documents, the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, considered that the declared price of the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, was significantly lower than the price risk parameters set by the Customs. Therefore, on November 27, 2002, Zhaoqing Customs issued a "Price Inquiry Notice" to Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, requesting a written explanation and the provision of relevant materials proving the truthfulness and accuracy of the declared price. On November 28 and 29, 2002, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company submitted to Zhaoqing Customs explanations regarding the business dealings between the overseas supplier, Hong Kong Aosi Company, and the domestic actual consignee, the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company; the agreement for Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company to act as an agent for importing electronic components; an explanation of the agency import by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company; the confirmation of sale signed between Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company; the "Price Declaration Form for Imported Goods of the Customs of the People's Republic of China"; import goods packing lists, invoices, and bills of lading; special value-added tax invoices for the same model integrated circuits issued by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company to Aosi Technology Company; purchase orders from several domestic companies to Aosi Technology Company or Yuema (Aosi); special value-added tax invoices for the same model integrated circuits issued by Aosi Technology Company to several domestic companies; and price information materials for integrated circuits from relevant integrated circuit agents, etc. From December 2002 to April 2003, Zhaoqing Customs further inquired about the declared price information of the imported goods through inquiries, consultations, and discussions with Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, and also learned about the price trends and information for the same model integrated circuits from the Guangzhou Commodity Price Information Office of the General Administration of Customs (hereinafter referred to as the Customs Price Office). Based on this, Zhaoqing Customs found that a special relationship existed between the buyer and seller of the imported goods (the domestic actual consignee and the overseas supplier), and that this special relationship might have affected the transaction price. Consequently, in accordance with Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures, it decided not to accept the declared price of the imported goods.

To determine the dutiable value, on March 3, 2003, the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, conducted a price consultation with the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company. On March 17, 2003, Zhaoqing Customs presided over a valuation discussion with Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company. On April 28, 2003, Zhaoqing Customs again issued a "Price Inquiry Notice" to Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, questioning whether the special relationship between the buyer and seller might have affected the transaction price. On May 12, 2003, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company submitted to Zhaoqing Customs 11 documents, including the "Supplementary Explanation on the Declared Price of Zhaoqing City Aosi Science and Technology Co., Ltd." After reviewing these materials, Zhaoqing Customs concluded that their credibility was low and they could not effectively prove that the declared import price was true, reasonable, and capable of serving as the basis for determining the dutiable value. On May 15, 2003, Zhaoqing Customs again conducted a price consultation with Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, but Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company consistently disagreed with the re-valuation of the imported goods. Because Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company failed to provide the materials necessary for determining the dutiable value using the transaction value of identical goods method, transaction value of similar goods method, deductive value method, and computed value method, and because Zhaoqing Customs also did not possess such price data, on May 20, 2003, after price inquiry, Zhaoqing Customs used a reasonable method to conduct the valuation and issued three "Tax Payment Certificates," deciding to collect value-added tax of RMB 13,172.08 on the three batches of integrated circuits declared by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company. Upon the application of Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, Zhaoqing Customs issued four "Valuation Notices" on May 28, 2003, informing Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company that: For RC4558DR and RC4558P type integrated circuits, Zhaoqing Customs decided to value them at USD 0.0898 each; for SN74HCU04DR type integrated circuits, Zhaoqing Customs decided to value them at USD 0.09 each. Each of the four "Valuation Notices" stated that the valuation was made in accordance with Article 34 and Article 7, paragraph 1, item (5) of the Customs Valuation Measures, and informed of the remedies available for challenging the valuation act. Dissatisfied with the decisions made in the three "Tax Payment Certificates" and the four "Valuation Notices," Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company applied to the Guangzhou Customs for administrative reconsideration. On November 25, 2003, after reconsideration, the Guangzhou Customs decided to uphold the three "Tax Payment Certificates" and the four "Valuation Notices" issued by Zhaoqing Customs.

It is further found that: For the integrated circuits declared for import by the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, the overseas seller was Hong Kong Aosi Company, and the domestic actual consignee was the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company. An agency relationship for import existed between Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, whereby Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company acted as an agent to import the relevant electronic components on behalf of Aosi Technology Company, handling matters such as signing contracts with foreign parties and customs declaration. Aosi Technology Company was jointly operated by Li Zhaohan, the registrant of Hong Kong Aosi Company, and Feng Weiheng, the legal representative of Aosi Technology Company. Part of Aosi Technology Company's working capital was provided by Hong Kong Aosi Company, maintaining a branch-head office relationship with Hong Kong Aosi Company. The two parties orally agreed that the sales profits of Aosi Technology Company would be distributed as follows: Aosi Technology Company would receive 30%, and Hong Kong Aosi Company would receive 70%.

The Zhaoqing Intermediate People's Court holds that:

1. Article 42, paragraph 1, item (3) of the Customs Valuation Measures stipulates that where one party, directly or indirectly, controls the other party, the buyer and seller shall be deemed to have a special relationship. On November 28, 2002, in its "Business Explanation regarding Aosi Technology Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company," the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, admitted that its relationship with the seller, Hong Kong Aosi Company, was that of a branch and head office. Additionally, on December 3 and December 10, 2002, in the interview record prepared by the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, and in Aosi Technology Company's "Explanation regarding Aosi Technology Company's Purchase and Sale of Integrated Circuits," Aosi Technology Company also admitted that it had a joint operation and profit-sharing arrangement with Hong Kong Aosi Company. Based on this evidence, Zhaoqing Customs correctly found that a special relationship existed between the buyer, Aosi Technology Company, and the seller, Hong Kong Aosi Company.

2. On March 17, 2003, at the Customs valuation discussion presided over by the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, and the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, admitted that the declared price of the goods in question was actually determined by Hong Kong Aosi Company. Although Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company attempted to use documents such as sales contracts, purchase orders, price inquiry sheets, and value-added tax invoices to prove that this declared price was true and reasonable, these documents contained varying degrees of contradictions and defects, failing to demonstrate their own truthfulness and reasonableness, and therefore could not serve to prove the truthfulness and reasonableness of the declared price. The opinion issued by the Customs Price Office stated that the declared price of the goods in question was lower than the actual comparable transaction prices of the same model integrated circuits known to the Customs, lower than the quotations on authoritative international integrated circuit websites, and lower than the production cost of the integrated circuits. As the professional management department for price information on imported goods subject to Customs control, the Customs Price Office possesses a vast amount of price information data. Compared to the materials provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, the price opinion issued by the Customs Price Office is more credible and should be accepted. Zhaoqing Customs correctly concluded based on this that the special relationship between the buyer and seller of the goods in question affected the transaction price.

3. Article 55, paragraph 1 of the Customs Law provides: "The dutiable value of import and export goods shall be examined and determined by the Customs based on the transaction value of the goods. Where the transaction value cannot be determined, the dutiable value shall be estimated by the Customs according to law." Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides: "Where the Customs has reason to believe that the special relationship between the buyer and seller has affected the transaction value, it shall inform the consignee of the imported goods in writing of the reasons, requiring the consignee to provide further explanation in writing, and to provide relevant materials or other evidence to prove that the relationship between the parties did not affect the transaction value. If, within 15 days from the date of issuance of the written notice by the Customs, the consignee of the imported goods fails to provide further explanation, or if the Customs still has reason to believe that the relationship between the buyer and seller affected the transaction value after reviewing the materials or evidence provided, the Customs may refuse to accept the declared value and shall determine the dutiable value in accordance with Articles 7 to 11 of these Measures." Pursuant to the above provisions, the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, has the authority to examine, determine, and estimate the dutiable value of imported goods. After concluding that the special relationship between the buyer and seller of the imported goods affected the transaction value, Zhaoqing Customs informed the consignee of the imported goods, the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, of this reason in writing. Within the statutory period, the evidence provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company could not prove that the special relationship between the buyer and seller did not affect the transaction value. Zhaoqing Customs therefore refused to accept the declared value of the imported goods and estimated the dutiable value according to law. Its enforcement action has a legal basis.

4. During the Customs valuation process, although the Plaintiff, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, and the Third Party, Aosi Technology Company, provided various materials including domestic sales contracts, purchase orders, price inquiry sheets, and value-added tax invoices, these materials contained contradictions and defects and had low credibility. Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company consistently failed to provide to the Defendant, Zhaoqing Customs, the records of foreign exchange payments that could directly reflect international trade prices or the international trade price data for the integrated circuit industry. Furthermore, the evidence provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company could not prove that the claimed price was the price at which the goods were sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to persons not having a special relationship in the domestic market, and lacked objectively quantifiable data for deduction items. Therefore, these materials could not serve as a basis for determining the dutiable value using the transaction value of similar goods method, the deductive value method, or the computed value method. Under such circumstances, after sequentially ruling out the various valuation methods stipulated in Article 7 of the Customs Valuation Measures, Zhaoqing Customs, referencing import prices of the same model integrated circuits at other ports and fully considering the interests of Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, used the actual transaction price data of goods with the same specifications and models as the basis and adopted a reasonable method to estimate the dutiable value. The procedure for its valuation was lawful and did not exceed the scope of administrative discretion.

Third Party Aosi Technology Company argued that during the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs' price verification process, it had already provided a large amount of information to Zhaoqing Customs through the Appellant Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company, and that this information was all true. However, Zhaoqing Customs neither actively investigated the authenticity of this information nor adopted it, which amounted to disregarding the rights of the administrative counterparty. As previously mentioned, where a special relationship exists between the buyer and seller and this special relationship affects the transaction value, Customs' adjustment of the declared price of imported goods is a power conferred on Customs by Article 55 of the Customs Law and Articles 7 and 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures. Regardless of whether the information provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company was true, as long as it could not prove that the transaction value was not affected by the special relationship between the buyer and seller, Zhaoqing Customs could lawfully adjust the declared price of the imported goods. Under this premise, whether Customs further needed to verify the authenticity of this information pertains to the reasonableness of the specific administrative act of the administrative agency and is not within the scope of review of administrative litigation.

In summary, the three Tax Payment Forms (on behalf of collection) and the four Valuation Notice Letters issued by the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs correctly applied laws and regulations, complied with statutory procedures, and should be upheld. Accordingly, the Zhaoqing Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC, on June 22, 2005, rendered the following judgment:

1. Uphold the three Tax Payment Forms (on behalf of collection) issued by the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs on May 20, 2003, and the four Valuation Notice Letters issued on May 28 of the same year;
2. Dismiss the other claims of the Appellant Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company.

The court acceptance fee for this case is RMB 100, to be borne by the Appellant Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, being dissatisfied, appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court. Their grounds for appeal were:
1. The capital verification report submitted by Aosi Technology Company proved that Hong Kong Aosi Company was not a shareholder of Aosi Technology Company, and thus there was no control relationship between them. The Respondent Zhaoqing Customs determined that the declared price was lower than the transaction value of identical or similar goods or international market price quotations, and that a special relationship existed between the buyer and seller affecting the transaction value, without any evidence to support these findings. That is, although the Respondent questioned the Appellant's declared price, it had no evidence to prove the grounds for its questioning. Under these circumstances, the first-instance judgment's finding that a special relationship existed between Aosi Technology Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company affecting the transaction value was an error in fact-finding.
2. Article 6 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides that even if a special relationship exists between the buyer and seller, if the consignee can prove that the declared price is close to the transaction value of identical or similar goods sold by the seller to unrelated buyers within the customs territory at the same time or approximately the same time, Customs shall accept the declared price. On the day the Appellant received the "Price Query Notice" from the Respondent, it provided relevant evidence to the Respondent. However, the Respondent failed to review this evidence and accept the transaction value, violating this provision.
3. The buyer and seller in this case were Aosi Technology Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company. Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company was merely the import agent for Aosi Technology Company. During the Customs price verification process, the Respondent did not list Aosi Technology Company, which had a direct interest in the specific administrative act, as an administrative counterparty, and did not issue the "Price Query Notice" to Aosi Technology Company, but instead issued it to Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company. This was erroneous.
4. After issuing the "Price Query Notice", the Respondent did not grant a 15-day period as required by Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures, resulting in Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company being unable to provide sufficient evidence.
5. Article 7 of the Customs Valuation Measures stipulates four methods for assessing customs value and requires that these methods must be used sequentially. During the process of determining the customs value, the Respondent did not follow the statutory order and directly used the reasonable method for valuation, seriously violating the law. The customs value assessed under these circumstances lacked sufficient basis and was essentially arbitrary.
6. The Respondent claimed it assessed the customs value using the reasonable method based on price data in Customs' possession. However, the Respondent refused to disclose the evidence relied upon for its valuation to the Appellants, citing that the price data was a Customs secret. The first-instance court also refused to conduct open cross-examination on this part of the evidence, citing trade secrets, which violated statutory procedures. The Appellants requested the revocation of the first-instance judgment, either remanding the case for retrial or, after ascertaining the facts, issuing a judgment revoking the four Valuation Notice Letters and the corresponding three Tax Payment Forms (on behalf of collection) issued by the Respondent.

The Respondent Zhaoqing Customs responded to the appeal, arguing that the three Tax Payment Forms (on behalf of collection) and the four Valuation Notice Letters issued to the Appellants were based on clear facts, conclusive evidence, correct application of law, and proper procedures. The Appellants' appeal was without factual and legal basis and should be dismissed, and the first-instance judgment upheld.

The Guangdong High People's Court, upon trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The focal points of dispute to be resolved in the second instance were:
1. Can it be determined that a special relationship existed between Hong Kong Aosi Company and Aosi Technology Company, and that this special relationship affected the transaction value?
2. After receiving the relevant evidence provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, should Zhaoqing Customs have accepted their declared price?
3. Was it erroneous for Zhaoqing Customs not to issue the "Price Query Notice" to Aosi Technology Company?
4. After Zhaoqing Customs issued the "Price Query Notice", did it fail to allow the parties 15 days to provide evidence and explanations?
5. Did Zhaoqing Customs' use of the reasonable method for valuation violate the provisions of Article 7 of the Customs Valuation Measures?
6. Did the first-instance court's refusal to conduct open cross-examination on the grounds that Customs' price data involved secrets violate statutory procedures?

The Guangdong High People's Court held:

I. Regarding the existence of a special relationship between the Appellant Aosi Technology Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company, the first-instance judgment had already listed the evidence upon which this finding was based. Article 42, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures stipulates eight circumstances that shall be deemed to constitute a special relationship between the buyer and seller, one of which is "one party directly or indirectly owns, controls, or holds 5% or more of the other party's outstanding voting shares or stocks." Although the capital verification report proved that Hong Kong Aosi Company was not a shareholder of Aosi Technology Company, this only reflects the registered capital situation of Aosi Technology Company and does not mean that no relationship existed between the two companies in actual business operations. The Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company denied the existence of a special relationship between Hong Kong Aosi Company and Aosi Technology Company on the grounds that the former was not a shareholder. This reason cannot be sustained.

II. Article 6, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides: "Where a special relationship exists between the buyer and seller, if Customs verifies that the special relationship has not affected the transaction value, or if the consignee of the imported goods can prove that the transaction value is close to any of the following prices prevailing at the same time or approximately the same time, Customs shall accept that transaction value: (1) the transaction value of identical or similar goods sold to unrelated buyers within the customs territory; (2) the customs value of identical or similar goods determined in accordance with Article 9 of these Measures; (3) the customs value of identical or similar goods determined in accordance with Article 10 of these Measures." After the special relationship between the Appellant Aosi Technology Company and Hong Kong Aosi Company was established, the Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company could only have the transaction value accepted by Customs if they proved that the transaction value met the conditions set forth in Article 6, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures. Although Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company provided a large amount of price data, these data contained varying degrees of contradictions and flaws and could not prove that the transaction value met the conditions set forth in Article 6, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures. Therefore, Zhaoqing Customs' refusal to accept the transaction value claimed by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company was legally justified.

III. Article 54 of the Customs Law provides: "The consignee of imported goods, the consignor of exported goods, and the owner of inbound and outbound articles are the taxpayers of customs duties." Article 31 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides: "The consignee or consignor of import or export goods shall truthfully declare to Customs the transaction value of the import or export goods and provide documents including invoices, contracts, packing lists, and other documents, written materials, and electronic data proving the truthfulness and completeness of the declared price. When Customs deems it necessary, the consignee or consignor of import or export goods shall also supplementarily declare to Customs information reflecting the relationship between the buyer and seller and the transaction activities, as well as other information related to the transaction value." The Appellant Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company was the consignee clearly recorded on the customs declaration forms for the imported goods in question. Based on this, the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs treated only Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company as the counterparty in administrative management and issued the "Price Query Notice" to that company. This was in compliance with legal provisions and did not constitute a procedural error.

IV. The Respondent Zhaoqing Customs issued the "Price Query Notice" to the Appellant Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company twice: first on November 27, 2002, and second on April 28, 2003. The three Tax Payment Forms (on behalf of collection) were issued on May 20, 2003, and the four Valuation Notice Letters were issued on May 28, 2003. Even calculating from the date the second "Price Query Notice" was issued, the time until the specific administrative acts were taken exceeded 15 days. The Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company's claim that Zhaoqing Customs did not allow 15 days after issuing the "Price Query Notice," violating the time limit stipulated in Article 34 of the Customs Valuation Measures, is without factual basis.

V. Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides: "Where the customs value of imported goods cannot be determined in accordance with Article 3 of these Measures, Customs shall, in the following order, use the following methods to assess the customs value: (1) transaction value of identical goods method; (2) transaction value of similar goods method; (3) deductive value method; (4) computed value method; (5) reasonable method." Articles 8 to 11 of the Customs Valuation Measures respectively stipulate the applicable conditions for each valuation method. The transaction value of identical or similar goods method shall be "based on the transaction value of identical or similar goods imported at the same time or approximately the same time as the goods being valued" and "shall first use the transaction value of identical or similar goods produced by the same producer; only in the absence of the transaction value of identical or similar goods produced by the same producer may the transaction value of identical or similar goods produced in the same country or region be used." Among the price data provided by the Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, there was no transaction value of identical or similar goods produced by the same producer. Furthermore, although the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs possessed price data for integrated circuits of the same model, they were not contemporaneous or approximately contemporaneous with the goods being valued, nor were they from the same country of production, thus failing to meet the applicable conditions for these two valuation methods. The deductive value method "shall be based on the selling price in the domestic market of the imported goods being valued, or identical or similar imported goods" and must simultaneously meet conditions such as "sold at or about the time of importation of the goods being valued," "sold in the condition as imported," "sold at the first commercial level within the customs territory," "representing the greatest aggregate quantity of sales," and "sold to unrelated parties within the customs territory." It also requires deductions for "profits and general expenses and commissions usually paid for sales within the customs territory of goods of the same class or kind," "transportation, insurance, loading and unloading, and other related costs incurred within the customs territory," and "import duties, import-stage taxes, and other domestic taxes related to the importation or sale of the goods." Although Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company provided VAT invoices for integrated circuits of the same model, upon review, these invoices contained multiple contradictions. Zhaoqing Customs considered that these invoices could hardly reflect the actual trade situation and could not prove that the claimed price represented the greatest aggregate quantity of sales within the territory, was sold to unrelated parties within the territory, or that objective quantifiable data on expenses to be deducted were provided. Although Zhaoqing Customs possessed sales prices for imported integrated circuits of the same model, these prices were not for sales at the first commercial level within the customs territory in the condition as imported, representing the greatest aggregate quantity of sales, and sold at or about the time of importation of the goods being valued, thus failing to meet the conditions for applying the deductive value method. The computed value method assesses the customs value of imported goods based on the sum of "the value of the materials and fabrication or other processing employed in producing the imported goods," "profit and general expenses equal to those reflected in the sale of goods of the same class or kind for export to the customs territory," and "the cost of transport and related charges, and insurance for the goods prior to their unloading at the place of entry within the customs territory." Applying this method also requires possession of objective quantifiable data regarding the foreign producer's costs, profits, expenses, etc. Since the information provided by Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company could hardly reflect the actual trade situation, and Customs also lacked this information, the conditions for applying the computed value method were absent. Article 11 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides that when using the reasonable method, Customs shall determine the customs value on the basis of data available within the customs territory, using the valuation principles of these Measures, but shall not use "the selling price of goods produced within the customs territory within the customs territory," "the higher of two alternative values," "the selling price of goods in the export market," "a price calculated based on a value or cost other than those specified in Article 10, paragraph 1 of these Measures," "the selling price of goods exported to a third country or region," or "minimum customs values or arbitrary or fictitious values." After sequentially eliminating the first four valuation methods, Zhaoqing Customs, using the reasonable method, conducted the valuation based on the actual import transaction price data for products of the same model and specification at other domestic ports in Customs' possession. This complied with the procedures stipulated in Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Customs Valuation Measures, also complied with the valuation principles stipulated in Article 11, and did not exceed the scope of the administrative agency's discretionary power.

VI. The price data for integrated circuits of the same model and specification, cited by the Respondent Zhaoqing Customs for raising price queries and determining the valuation, originated from the import prices of other enterprises and involved the trade secrets of those enterprises. Article 38 of the Customs Valuation Measures provides: "Customs shall keep confidential any information provided by the buyer, seller, or trade-related parties that constitutes a trade secret." Article 37 of the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Administrative Litigation provides: "Evidence involving state secrets, trade secrets, personal privacy, or other evidence that should be kept confidential as provided by law shall not be openly cross-examined during court sessions." The first-instance court correctly handled the portion of evidence submitted by Zhaoqing Customs that Customs was obligated to keep confidential by not conducting open cross-examination. The Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company's claim that this violated statutory procedures is unfounded.

In summary, the first-instance judgment was based on clear facts, sufficient evidence, and an appropriate decision. The grounds for appeal of the Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company cannot be sustained and should be dismissed according to law. The Guangdong High People's Court, pursuant to Article 61(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC, on November 24, 2005, rendered the following judgment:

Appeal dismissed; the first-instance judgment is affirmed.

The court acceptance fee for the second instance is RMB 100, to be borne equally by the Appellants Zhaoqing Foreign Trade Company and Aosi Technology Company, each paying RMB 50.

This judgment is final.
